faq.a: Only hepatic adenoma has a small risk of malignant transformation, especially >5 cm or in the presence of cirrhosis.
faq.q: Can a benign liver tumour become cancerous?

faq.a: Rarely; only when imaging is inconclusive and the result will change management.
Avoid alcohol excess, stop oral contraceptives or anabolic steroids, and vaccinate against hepatitis B.
faq.q: What lifestyle advice should be given?

exam: What imaging feature distinguishes a haemangioma from focal nodular hyperplasia? — Peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill‑in for haemangioma; central scar with homogeneous arterial enhancement for FNH.

A 28‑year‑old woman on combined oral contraceptives has a 4 cm liver lesion with arterial hyperenhancement and wash‑out. What is the most likely diagnosis and next step? — Hepatic adenoma; advise stopping contraceptives and arrange surveillance or resection if lesion enlarges.

How does chronic hepatitis B infection affect the work‑up of a newly discovered liver mass? — Raises suspicion for HCC; obtain AFP and consider contrast CT/MRI even if the lesion appears benign on ultrasound.
When is surgical resection indicated for a hepatic haemangioma? — Lesion >5 cm with pain, risk of rupture, or rapid growth; also if diagnosis remains uncertain.
What is the role of trans‑arterial embolisation in benign liver tumours? — Used to shrink large haemangiomas when surgery is contraindicated; reduces risk of rupture.

A patient presents with sudden right‑upper‑quadrant pain and hypotension. Ultrasound shows a large liver lesion with free fluid. What is the likely complication and immediate management? — Rupture of a haemangioma; resuscitate, arrange urgent surgical or interventional radiology control of bleeding.
Why is AFP not a reliable sole test to exclude malignancy in endemic hepatitis regions? — AFP can be normal in early HCC; imaging and clinical risk factors must be integrated.
What key history points help differentiate FNH from hepatic adenoma? — Absence of oral contraceptive use, lack of metabolic disease, and typical imaging central scar favor FNH.
ai.title: Benign Liver Tumors
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Benign liver tumours are usually asymptomatic lesions that require differentiation from malignant disease. Management focuses on accurate diagnosis, monitoring, and selective intervention in symptomatic or high‑risk cases.

b: Most are incidentally found on ultrasound or CT performed for other reasons.
Malignancy risk is low, but mis‑diagnosis can lead to unnecessary surgery.
sections.p: Benign liver tumours are non‑cancerous growths arising from hepatocytes, bile ducts, or vascular tissue. The three common types in low‑resource settings are hepatic haemangioma, focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH) and hepatic adenoma.

b: Haemangioma: peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill‑in on contrast imaging.
FNH: central scar with homogeneous arterial enhancement, iso‑intense on delayed phases.
Adenoma: arterial phase hyperenhancement, wash‑out on portal venous phase; associated with oral contraceptives, anabolic steroids, glycogen storage disease.
sections.p: Diagnosis relies on imaging patterns and clinical context. In tropical regions, consider co‑existing liver disease (hepatitis B/C, schistosomiasis) that may alter imaging or raise suspicion for cancer.

b: Risk factors for malignant transformation: size >5 cm, rapid growth, background cirrhosis, hepatitis B/C infection.
In low‑resource hospitals, lack of MRI may require reliance on ultrasound and clinical judgment.
sections.p: Most patients are asymptomatic; large lesions may cause abdominal discomfort, early satiety, or rare rupture (especially haemangioma). The main clinical task is to rule out hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) or metastasis.

t.b: Is the lesion cystic, solid, vascular? – Typical haemangioma shows well‑defined hyperechoic mass; FNH appears iso‑echoic with central scar.
What is the enhancement pattern? – Helps differentiate haemangioma, FNH, adenoma, and HCC.
Is there a marker of HCC? – Normal AFP supports benign lesion; markedly elevated (>400 ng/mL) suggests HCC.

t.a: Liver function tests (ALT, AST, ALP, bilirubin)
t.b: Are liver enzymes abnormal? – Significant elevation may indicate underlying hepatitis or tumour necrosis.

t.a: If CT unavailable, repeat focused ultrasound with contrast agents (if affordable)
t.b: Can we improve lesion characterization? – Contrast‑enhanced US can mimic CT patterns for haemangioma and FNH.

b: Observation: repeat ultrasound every 6–12 months; no treatment needed if stable.
Surgical resection: indicated for haemangioma >5 cm with pain or risk of rupture, or for adenoma in women planning pregnancy.
Trans‑arterial embolisation: option for large haemangioma when surgery is high risk.
Avoid oral contraceptives or anabolic steroids in hepatic adenoma.
sections.p: Most benign tumours are observed. Intervention is reserved for symptomatic lesions, size >5 cm, or uncertain diagnosis.

b: Hepatocellular carcinoma – usually shows arterial hyperenhancement with rapid wash‑out; AFP often raised.
Metastatic disease – multiple lesions, variable enhancement, history of extra‑hepatic cancer.
sections.p: Malignant liver lesions can mimic benign tumours on imaging, especially in cirrhotic livers.

b: Normal AFP does not completely exclude HCC; combine imaging and clinical risk factors.
Ultrasound may miss deep lesions; consider CT if suspicion persists.
sections.p: In endemic hepatitis B, small HCC may appear iso‑intense and be mistaken for adenoma.

b: Size >5 cm is the key threshold for considering resection of haemangioma.
Oral contraceptive use is a red flag for hepatic adenoma.
A central scar on imaging points toward FNH, not adenoma.
sections.p: Focus on differentiating imaging patterns, recognising when to intervene, and understanding the impact of co‑existing tropical liver disease.

b: Assuming all hyperechoic lesions are haemangioma without confirming enhancement pattern.
Missing the need for follow‑up imaging when a lesion is atypical.
sections.p: Errors often arise from over‑reliance on a single test or ignoring local disease prevalence.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain suggesting tumour rupture
Rapid increase in lesion size on serial imaging
New onset jaundice or liver failure
